How to choose, in one paragraph

If the destination is a browser you control, use WebP: it is the best balance of size, quality and support. If something outside your control will read the file (email, print, a marketplace, an old CMS), use JPG. If you need transparency or pixel-exact detail such as screenshots and text, use PNG. If you want the absolute smallest file and can accept slower encoding, use AVIF. And if the requirement is a hard number of kilobytes rather than a look, use one of the compress-to-size pages, those search for the quality that fits your ceiling instead of making you guess.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need to install anything?

No. Every tool runs inside your browser using WebAssembly builds of the same encoders professional tools use. There is no install, no account and no upload, and after the first visit it keeps working offline.

Which format should I convert to?

WebP for anything shown in a browser you control, JPG when something outside your control reads the file, PNG when you need transparency or pixel-exact detail like screenshots and text, and AVIF when you want the smallest possible file and can accept slower encoding.

Is there a file size or count limit?

No server-imposed limit, because there is no server. The practical ceiling is your own device's memory. Batches are capped at 200 files with a confirmation prompt above that.

Can I hit an exact file size?

Yes. The compress-to-size pages let you set a KB ceiling and the encoder searches quality until the output fits at or under it, rather than making you guess a quality number.

Are my images really not uploaded?

Correct. You can verify it yourself: open your browser's developer tools, watch the Network tab, and convert a file, no image data is transmitted. That is also why it works with no internet connection after the first load.

Is it free?

Yes, completely, with no caps, watermarks or accounts. It is supported by voluntary contributions rather than ads or tracking.
